curriculum.lesson_evidence: For many First Nations Peoples, Country means much more than land. It includes waters, sky, plants, animals, people, stories and responsibilities, and caring for Country is shared between people and place. Each Nation has its own relationship with its own Country, so we learn from local voices and published sources instead of assuming.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
A classmate says Country just means a piece of land. Using the ideas above, write one sentence that corrects the idea and name where you found your information.

FEEDBACK
Country includes land, waters, sky, living things and people, along with stories and responsibilities. Name the published source or the local educator who provided the idea.

WATCH FOR
Treating Country as only a place on a map misses the relationships and responsibilities described by First Nations authors and Custodians.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Read or listen to a published text by a First Nations author or local educator about Country. Record three ideas and the source. Then draw a place you belong to and write two sentences about how you care for it. Do not claim to know any Nation's ties to its Country.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.

FEEDBACK
Country includes land, waters, sky, living things and people, along with stories and responsibilities. Name the published source or the local educator who provided the idea.

It includes waters, sky, plants, animals, people, stories and responsibilities, and caring for Country is shared between people and place. Each Nation has its own relationship with its own Country, so we learn from local voices and published sources instead of assuming.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
